original.title: How New Zealand Hunted Its Own Kiwi

scenes.narration: New Zealand released stoats to save its sheep pastures. Why did the kiwi pay the price?. A stoat crosses the forest floor far from any rabbit, a native bird's egg broken beneath it. Sheep farmers here faced ruin. Rabbits, brought in decades before, had overrun the pasture, stripping it bare. So, as early as 1879, mustelids were turned loose to hunt them down.

event.text: All three mustelid species were introduced to New Zealand as early as 1879 to control rabbits that were destroying sheep pasture.

changes_state.from: Rabbits are multiplying and destroying sheep pasture across the New Zealand countryside.
changes_state.to: Settlers see the rabbits as an economic emergency demanding a solution.

scenes.narration: Ornithologists begged them to stop. Releasing a fierce new hunter, they warned, would not end with rabbits. The warnings were brushed aside, and in 1884 stoats were shipped in and let go.

event.text: Despite protests from ornithologists, stoats were imported and released in New Zealand in 1884 to control the rabbits.

changes_state.from: Rabbits are the target; stoats are not yet present in the wild.
changes_state.to: Live stoats are released into the New Zealand landscape as a rabbit control measure.

scenes.narration: The hunters did not stay in rabbit country.
They poured into the forests, places that held no rabbits at all. And there they found something slower. Ground-dwelling birds that could barely fly, nesting low, with eggs sitting out in the open.

event.text: Stoats spread quickly to forests and other areas where there were no rabbits, and fed on poorly flighted birds and their eggs.

changes_state.from: Stoats are expected to hunt rabbits on the pasture.
changes_state.to: Stoats are in the native forest, eating birds and eggs the rabbit plan never considered.

scenes.narration: For a predator, it was effortless. The birds had never faced a climbing, sniffing mammal before, so their eggs and chicks became an easy meal. A hunter imported for rabbits now fed on native wings.

event.text: Stoats spread quickly to forests and other areas where there were no rabbits, and fed on poorly flighted birds and their eggs.

changes_state.from: Stoats are expected to hunt rabbits on the pasture.
changes_state.to: Stoats are in the native forest, eating birds and eggs the rabbit plan never considered.

scenes.narration: Watch what this did to the kiwi. In a study of brown kiwi in central Northland, researchers tracked chicks to see what killed them. Where the killer could be named, stoats topped the list.

event.text: In a central Northland study of brown kiwi, stoats were the single largest identified cause of chick death, killing 19 of 31 chicks (63%) where the agent could be identified.

changes_state.from: Kiwi chicks hatch in forests now patrolled by an introduced hunter.
changes_state.to: Stoats account for 63% of identified chick deaths in the study area.

scenes.narration: Of thirty-one chicks whose deaths could be traced, nineteen were taken by stoats. Nearly two in three. One animal, released to thin the rabbits, had become the chief executioner of a forest bird.

event.text: In a central Northland study of brown kiwi, stoats were the single largest identified cause of chick death, killing 19 of 31 chicks (63%) where the agent could be identified.

changes_state.from: Kiwi chicks hatch in forests now patrolled by an introduced hunter.
changes_state.to: Stoats account for 63% of identified chick deaths in the study area.

scenes.narration: Zoom out from that one site. Researchers pooled study after study across the whole mainland, hunting for the single factor behind the kiwi's long slide. One thread ran through nearly all of it.

event.text: A meta-analysis found that the critical factor in the decline of kiwi on the New Zealand mainland was predation by introduced mammals, especially stoats killing kiwi chicks.

changes_state.from: Stoat predation is heavy in one local study.
changes_state.to: Stoat predation on chicks is identified as the critical driver of mainland kiwi decline.

scenes.narration: Predation by introduced mammals. Not disease, not logging, not bad luck. The critical driver of the kiwi's mainland collapse was the imported hunters, above all stoats, killing the chicks before they could grow up.

event.text: A meta-analysis found that the critical factor in the decline of kiwi on the New Zealand mainland was predation by introduced mammals, especially stoats killing kiwi chicks.

changes_state.from: Stoat predation is heavy in one local study.
changes_state.to: Stoat predation on chicks is identified as the critical driver of mainland kiwi decline.

scenes.narration: So here is where the rabbit fix has left the kiwi. In Northland today, only about one brown kiwi chick in twenty lives long enough to grow up, most of the rest lost to stoats and feral cats.

event.text: Only about 5% of Northland's brown kiwi chicks now reach adulthood, with their biggest threats being predation from stoats and feral cats.

changes_state.from: Kiwi once bred in forests without mammalian predators.
changes_state.to: Only about 5% of chicks survive to adulthood, with stoats among the top threats.

scenes.narration: That ratio is the quiet collapse. Nineteen in twenty vanish into the undergrowth long before they can breed, taken mostly by stoats and feral cats prowling the same forest floor.

event.text: Only about 5% of Northland's brown kiwi chicks now reach adulthood, with their biggest threats being predation from stoats and feral cats.

changes_state.from: Kiwi once bred in forests without mammalian predators.
changes_state.to: Only about 5% of chicks survive to adulthood, with stoats among the top threats.

scenes.narration: You might think the fix is simple: lay traps, set bait, clear the predator out. But the stoat is a hard animal to catch. It is cautious, and it does not trust what it did not find itself.

event.text: Stoats are difficult to control because they are clever and careful and very suspicious of baits and traps.

changes_state.from: Managers try to remove stoats to save chicks.
changes_state.to: Stoats evade baits and traps, making control costly and difficult to sustain.

scenes.narration: A clumsy trap teaches it nothing but suspicion. One bad scent, one wrong placement, and the animal learns the lesson for life, skirting every box you set from then on.

event.text: Stoats are difficult to control because they are clever and careful and very suspicious of baits and traps.

changes_state.from: Managers try to remove stoats to save chicks.
changes_state.to: Stoats evade baits and traps, making control costly and difficult to sustain.

scenes.narration: So pick up that opening image again. A stoat with something in its jaws, brought here to carry off rabbits that ate the pasture. Watch what it actually carries now.
Not a rabbit. A kiwi chick. The hunter did its job, just not the one the planners wrote down. When you import a hunter, who gets to decide what it hunts?
